identity.title: Position: AI Safety should prioritize the Future of Work

problem.claim: AI safety policy should account for AI’s effects on work, livelihoods, labor markets, and human agency.

gap.claim: The authors argue that prevailing AI safety priorities underemphasize human-centric, long-term societal consequences, especially the future of work.

contributions.claim: Recommends comprehensive transition support toward meaningful labor with human agency.
Uses economic theories to frame AI’s intertemporal effects on livelihoods and labor-market changes associated with greater income inequality.
Advocates collective licensing, fair compensation for training data, and a pro-worker framework for global AI governance.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper’s stated distinction is to prioritize the future of work as a central AI-safety concern and to connect this priority with transition support and pro-worker governance.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that structural labor-market changes linked to AI exacerbate income inequality.
The authors characterize major stakeholders’ closed-source approach as resembling rent-seeking through resource exploitation, degraded creative labor, and monopolized innovation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Describes current AI-safety priorities as harmful-content filtering, manipulation prevention, and existential cyber- or biosecurity risks.
Argues that this focus overlooks human-centered factors shaping society’s long-term trajectory.
Identifies future-of-work risks and recommends transition support preserving meaningful labor and human agency.
Uses economic theory to discuss livelihood effects, labor-market restructuring, and inequality.
Critiques closed-source development and proposes collective licensing plus pro-worker global governance.

source_observation.claim: The paper links its central priority claim to both an explanatory lens on labor-market change and concrete governance mechanisms.

lessons.interpretation: A position paper can make a broad agenda actionable by pairing diagnosis with institutional proposals.
lessons.application: When advancing a neglected risk priority, connect the risk mechanism to specific support, compensation, or governance instruments.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the proposed instruments depend on empirical or legal details absent from the available evidence.

unknowns: The abstract does not report empirical studies, formal proofs, or detailed economic estimates.
It does not specify how collective licensing would be designed or implemented internationally.
The claims about rent-seeking and inequality are author-reported and cannot be independently assessed from the abstract.
